resolution: Recorded in the cross-check report as 'exchange prints 21/24' for 2026-09-14; the collector re-requests with an explicit fromdate so a later run can fill the gap, and the affected sessions are listed in the rollover ladder rather than assumed.

topic: FRED SP500 had not published 2026-09-18 while NASDAQCOM and DJIA had
detail: At collection time the official composite series for the session of 2026-09-18 existed (NASDAQCOM 26,522.550, DJIA 51,682.640) but the S&P 500 series - the calendar authority this project builds its session list from - still ended on 2026-09-17 (7,637.76), as did VIXCLS, SOFR, DGS10 and DGS3MO. A session can therefore be tradable by the exchange's record and still be outside the official calendar, and the two states must not be presented as the same thing.
resolution: The rollover ladder labels 2026-09-18 PROVISIONAL-EXCHANGE-PRINTS and lists exactly which official series are missing. The book settles on it, every fill records 'session_verification' and 'session_official_missing', and a later run upgrades the label to a collected-calendar session once SP500 publishes its observation. No fill is ever labelled as an official-calendar settlement when it is not one.

topic: DCOILWTICO and DTWEXBGS are missing from the forward sessions by publication frequency, not by collection failure
detail: The WTI spot series ended on 2026-09-15 and the broad dollar index has no 2026-09-18 observation, so two of the nine registered official series cannot confirm a forward session even after every business day has passed. Presenting 'official series missing' without saying which misses are structural would overstate the gap.
resolution: The ladder lists the series by identifier and the summary page states that these two are weekly/low-frequency reporters. The evidence block in the market records each series with its own last observation date, and no proxy or interpolation is substituted.

topic: The forward print rows are transcribed from two publishers in a session with no outbound HTTPS
detail: The development sandbox cannot open an HTTPS connection, so the 2026-09-14..18 rows for all 24 symbols were retrieved through the page-fetch path and transcribed into data/real/prints/raw/. Both publishers were read for every symbol and every session, and the two transcriptions agree to 0.0005 bps on closes over 117 symbol-sessions, which is strong evidence against a transcription slip - but it is evidence, not a byte-exact raw response, and an earlier revision of the collector also had a shared-timestamp bug that could only misalign rows silently.
resolution: The scheduled rollover workflow (live-rollover.yml) re-fetches both endpoints over HTTPS on a runner and writes the raw bytes it received, so the repository's custodian record for 2026-09-14..18 is replaced by a runner-fetched one on its first run. The transcribed rows keep the publisher's own strings, the request URL and the retrieval time, and no row is accepted unless both publishers agree within 5 bps.

topic: The custody chain for the 2026-09-19 writes was recorded after the writes
detail: Thirty collected files changed on 2026-09-19 between 04:11Z and 04:25Z: the collector re-fetched three FRED windows and regenerated two derived index documents, the forward collector appended 2026-09-17/18 to all 24 Yahoo price files, and the price audit rewrote the eligibility report. The Season 2 run had already recorded the SHA-256 of every one of those files, so its custody checks then failed 54 of 2,682 checks - and nothing noticed, because the Season 2 auditor existed but was not wired into CI. The fix has two halves: sim/custody.py now logs (previous hash, new hash, writer, reason) as a writer changes a file, and scripts/collect_forward_prints.py plus scripts/collect_real_data.py call it at the moment of the write. For the 30 writes that had already happened, the chain rows were reconstructed from the hashes the run recorded together with each file's own modification time, and every one of them says so in utc_source. That is weaker evidence than a row written by the writer as it wrote, which is why it is filed here rather than presented as a write log.
resolution: 24 of the 30 files are byte-reconstructible: removing the appended sessions reproduces the recorded hash exactly, so the change is proven rather than asserted. The other six (three FRED CSVs, collection_manifest.json, coverage_report.json, official_price_eligibility.json) are regenerations whose previous bytes are gone; for those the chain row is an explanation by the project, not a receipt, and the audit prints them as chained rather than as byte-identical. Landed: sim/custody.py logs every write to a collected file as it happens, both collectors call it, the Season 2 auditor now accepts a chained change only when the chain ends at the bytes on disk, and the audit is wired into CI so the next drift cannot pass unnoticed.

topic: The insider bulk collector asked the wrong layout first for every quarter
detail: The SEC serves the quarterly Form 3/4/5 data sets from two directory layouts, and its own page states the change: the 2026 Q2 set lives under files/datastandardsinnovation/ and 2026 Q1 and earlier under files/structureddata/. The collector tried the older layout first for every quarter and only the newest one was actually collected, so the order cost one wasted request per quarter per run - and, more importantly, left the register citing the layout the publisher no longer uses for recent files.
resolution: sim/sec.py now carries both layouts as named endpoints and a insider_zip_candidates(quarter) helper that puts the layout the SEC's table names for that quarter's date range first, with the other as a fallback; the collector calls that helper instead of keeping its own copy of the patterns, and tests/test_sec_access.py pins the order, the change quarter and the fallback for an unparseable quarter.

topic: The fee claim text asserted a $0.01 minimum on the equity TAF that the primary schedule does not contain
detail: The verified-sources register in sim/config.py described the FINRA Trading Activity Fee as '$0.000195 per share on equity sells (minimum $0.01, maximum $9.79) from 2026-01-01'. Re-reading FINRA's own fee-adjustment schedule (SR-FINRA-2024-019) and Schedule A Section 1 on 2026-09-19 shows the covered-equity line carries a per-trade MAXIMUM only; the minimum applies to security-futures round turns. The numeric schedules were always correct (rate_for() applies rate and cap only), so no computed fee changed - the defect was in the claim sentence a reviewer was told to trust.
resolution: sim/config.py claim text corrected to state no equity minimum and name the rule it was confused with; sim/venue_admin.regulator_fees() documents the same; tests/test_venue_admin.py pins the arithmetic for the small-execution exemption.

topic: An official source URL moved and now returns 404: FRBservices holiday schedule
detail: https://www.frbservices.org/resources/holidays - the Federal Reserve settlement-holiday page - returned a 404 page on 2026-09-19; the live page is now https://www.frbservices.org/about/holiday-schedules. This is exactly the failure mode the planned cite-hygiene job targets: a link that was correct when first recorded rots silently.
resolution: sim/venue_admin.py records only the live URL with its 2026-09-19 check date; the stale path is documented here so the citation chain stays honest rather than silently swapped.

topic: FINRA's own pages disagree across publication dates: By-Laws rule text shows the pre-2026 TAF rate while the dated fee-adjustment schedule shows the operative 2026 rate
detail: https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/rulebooks/corporate-organization/section-1-member-regulatory-fees (Schedule A, Section 1) displayed $0.000166 per share / $8.30 cap on 2026-09-19, while the same publisher's fee-adjustment schedule states the operative 2026 values $0.000195 / $9.79. A project that reads only the rule text would undercost 2026 sales. This is version skew inside an official publisher's site, not an aggregator error.
resolution: sim/config.py's dated schedules (FINRA_TAF_PER_SHARE, FINRA_TAF_MAX_PER_TRADE) follow the dated fee-adjustment schedule, which is the operative rate; the rulebook page remains linked as rule text with the skew noted in the row and here.

topic: The collector's new marker gate fired on its own documentation: the trigger string appeared in the commit body that explained the gate
detail: collect-real-data.yml gates push-triggered runs on contains(head_commit.message, '[collect-data]'). github.event.head_commit.message is the FULL commit message, and the very commit that introduced the gate explained the marker in its body - so the gate correctly matched and started a collection from a push that was only a workflow edit. Two runs queued in the same concurrency group (cancel-in-progress is false) and both collected; the collection is idempotent per date, so the cost was time, not correctness.
resolution: No code change needed - the gate did what it says. Recorded so future commit messages keep the marker out of explanatory prose; marker pushes should carry it in the subject line only.

topic: SEC insider bulk ZIPs: 'Request Rate Threshold Exceeded' is a pacing failure, not an identity failure
detail: All 16 insider-ZIP requests in the 2026-09-18 run (8 quarters x 2 documented layouts) returned HTTP 403 with SEC's 'Request Rate Threshold Exceeded' page, timestamps 5 seconds apart at ~3+ requests/second from a GitHub runner (cloud IP). The error body is the discriminator: 'Undeclared Automated Tool' would mean the User-Agent fix failed, while 'Rate Threshold' means the requests were understood but too fast. The declared-UA fix had landed; the pacing had not been adjusted for large-file bulk downloads. Follow-up, 2026-09-19 run: even at 1.2s pacing with 20s backoffs and zero prior sec.gov traffic in the run, the FIRST www.sec.gov ZIP request was already answered with the rate-threshold page - the shared GitHub-runner IP pool is throttled as such, not per-client. Worse, the 3-attempt/20s-backoff retries on 16 URLs consumed the run's remaining time budget, so the sections scheduled after insider_bulk (per-filing walk, FDA, sports, injury archive, weather, Kalshi) never started at all; the budget-exhausted flag was true and nba_scoreboard.jsonl stayed empty without a single ESPN request being made.
resolution: Three-part fix, landed 2026-09-19, with the 2026-09-20 run (35477020017) as the proof point: (1) the dcm.sec.gov host the data.gov catalog names was tried first on every quarter - it does not resolve at all from a GitHub runner (DNS 'Name or service not known', status 0 on all 16 attempts), so the catalog's download buttons are effectively dead for public DNS; (2) www.sec.gov answered every attempt with the rate-threshold page even at 1.2s pacing, 2 tries and 20s backoffs, with the sub-budget correctly bounding the section (budget_exhausted=false, every other section ran); (3) even the company_tickers.json map 403s from the runner. Conclusion, now proven rather than suspected: the SEC's bulk insider data sets are unreachable from shared GitHub-hosted runner IPs by any request shape this collector can send - the remaining paths are an owner-operated collection from a clean IP (self-hosted runner or a local run of scripts/collect_real_data.py --only insider_bulk,sec, which writes the same manifest and commits the same way) or waiting out the IP pool's reputation. The insider personas correctly stay flat; the register carries the caveat.

topic: ESPN's bare-season-year scoreboard looks complete and is not: the response is capped at ~25 events
detail: The daily-calendar sports (basketball, baseball) ignore the week parameter that fills the football files, and the obvious replacement - a bare season year, dates=2026 - answers HTTP 200 with a payload that looks like the whole season. It is not: the 2026-09-20 run's manifest records 340,836 bytes for the NBA request whose only events were 25 games from 2026-01-01 to 2026-01-04 (the season ran 2025-10-21 to 2026-06), and the baseball variant returned only spring-training games, which the preseason filter correctly dropped to zero rows. A naive reader would have committed 25 games as 'the NBA season'. The probe that suggested the form worked (a page-fetcher rendering of the same URL) could not distinguish a capped payload from a complete one - only the collected bytes and row dates could.
resolution: The only form verified to return a complete answer for a daily sport is a single calendar date (dates=20251021 returned that day's completed games with final scores; ranges, dates=YYYYMMDD-YYYYMMDD, answer HTTP 400). collect_espn now walks basketball and baseball day by day across the dates each season can intersect the trading window (NBA 2025-10-01..2026-06-30, MLB 2026-02-20..2026-09-16), preseason events are dropped to match the football weeks' seasontype coverage, and the request-form tests assert the walk spans so a silent revert to a capped form fails the suite.
